lines.en: What every good storyteller knows is that the ending must feel both surprising and inevitable.
It is not the events themselves that make a story, but the order in which they are revealed.
Had the novel opened with the funeral, the reader would have understood everything too soon.
What the old sailor never mentioned was the reason he had stopped going to sea.
Not until the final chapter do we learn that the narrator has been lying to us all along.
However simple the plot may seem, it is the silences between the scenes that carry the emotion.
It is said that every family has one story that is told at every gathering, and one that never is.
Were the story told from the villain's point of view, we might find ourselves forgiving him.
Little by little, the details fall into place, and what seemed a confusion turns out to be a design.
Rarely does the first version of a story survive; the best ones are told and retold until they shine.
What the grandmother's stories never explained was why she always stopped at the same point and smiled.
It is in the second telling that a story finds its true shape, the first being little more than a rehearsal.
Had the detective noticed the mud on the carpet in chapter one, the mystery would have lasted four pages.
What the film achieves without a single word of dialogue is more than most scripts manage in two hours.
Not until the last page does the reader understand why the story began in the middle.
